h1: The 5 Best Mesh WiFi Systems Under $100, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Mesh WiFi System Under $100: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 5 TP-Link Deco mesh WiFi systems that fit a $100 budget, compared on WiFi 6, pack size, backhaul and coverage claims.
summary: The TP-Link Deco X25 3-pack is the mesh WiFi system to buy under $100 if you want three nodes and WiFi 6, though it is sold renewed. The Deco X55 offers faster AX3000 hardware as a single unit, the Deco S4 3-pack is the older AC1900 value route, and the Deco X15 is the stretch pick with Ethernet backhaul.
intro: The cheapest way to ruin a mesh network is to buy the biggest pack you can afford and ignore where the nodes will sit. Mesh nodes pass traffic to each other over the air, so every hop between them costs speed. A three-pack placed badly can feel slower than a single good router in the middle of the house.

This ranking is about getting the best coverage for a $100 budget, and the honest answer is that at this price you are buying either older WiFi 5 hardware or discounted and renewed WiFi 6. We reviewed five TP-Link Deco systems from their listings, focusing on WiFi generation, pack size, ports and backhaul options. We left out standalone range extenders, which are a different kind of product and do not create a true mesh.

products.name: TP-Link - Deco X25 AX1800 Dual-Band Whole Home Mesh Wi-Fi 6 System (3-Pack) - White (Renewed)
products.verdict: Three WiFi 6 nodes under $100, with the catch that this unit is sold renewed.
products.description:
The Deco X25 is an AX1800 dual-band WiFi 6 mesh system, and this listing is a 3-pack. Three nodes is the right starting point for a typical two-story home, because it lets you place one near the modem, one at the far end of the same floor and one upstairs.

It ranks first because getting WiFi 6 and three nodes within $50 to $100 is the strongest value in the category. The AX1800 label describes the combined speed of the two bands, and it is enough for streaming and video calls across a normal household. It sits above the X55 because a full mesh set beats a single box for anyone with more than a small apartment. The tradeoff is the word renewed. A refurbished unit has had a previous owner, and the warranty coverage differs from a new one.

Buy it if you want whole-home coverage on a firm budget and are comfortable with refurbished gear. Read the seller's return window before ordering.

products.name: TP-Link Deco X55 AX3000 WiFi 6 Mesh System, Deco X55(1-Pack)
products.verdict: A faster AX3000 WiFi 6 unit that works alone and grows into a mesh later.
products.description:
The Deco X55 is an AX3000 WiFi 6 mesh system sold here as a single unit. AX3000 sits a tier above the AX1800 class, so each node has more headroom for fast internet plans and crowded networks.

It takes second place because speed per node is its strength, while a single node is also its limit. One unit covers a small home or apartment on its own, and you can add more Deco units later to extend it. That makes it a fair starting point, but it means that to equal the X25's three nodes you would be spending much more than $100. It beats the S4 packs on WiFi generation and raw speed.

Choose it if your home is compact and your internet plan is fast enough that an AX1800 would hold you back. Skip it for a larger house where one node cannot reach every room.

products.idealFor: Apartments and small homes on faster internet plans.

products.name: TP-Link Deco S4 Mesh AC1900 WiFi System, Deco S4(3-Pack)
products.verdict: An older AC1900 WiFi 5 set with three nodes for the budget-minded.
products.description:
The Deco S4 is an AC1900 mesh system in a 3-pack. The AC label marks it as WiFi 5, the generation before WiFi 6, so the radios handle fewer simultaneous devices and the efficiency gains of the newer standard are absent.

It ranks third because three nodes at this price still cover a large home, and plenty of households do not need WiFi 6 yet. If most of your devices are older phones, laptops and streaming sticks, the practical difference is small. It sits behind the renewed X25 because that model gives the same number of nodes with a newer standard. The advantage here is that you know what you are getting, and a new-condition pack may suit buyers who dislike refurbished gear.

Pick it for a larger home with modest demands. Skip it if you own many WiFi 6 devices or plan to keep the system for many years.

Older standard still handles everyday streaming and browsing fine

products.name: TP-Link Deco S4 Whole Home Mesh WiFi System, Deco S4(2-Pack)
products.verdict: Two Deco S4 nodes for medium homes, with no speed detail in the listing.
products.description:
This is the 2-pack of the Deco S4 whole-home mesh system. The listing is sparse and points buyers to the current page for the specs, so the clearest facts are the product line and the two-node count.

It ranks fourth because two nodes suit a medium home or a long single-floor layout, and the S4 line is a proven budget design. It falls behind the 3-pack because it covers less ground for similar money, and the extra node is the cheapest way to improve a mesh. Compared with the WiFi 6 options, the S4 is dated, which is the price of its low cost.

Buy it for a single-story house of modest size. If you suspect you will need more coverage, buy the 3-pack from the start, since adding one node later often costs more.

products.name: TP-Link Deco X15 Dual-Band AX1500 WiFi 6 Mesh Wi-Fi System | Replaces Routers and Extenders | Covers up to 5,600 sq.ft. | 2 Gigabit Ports...
products.verdict: A WiFi 6 AX1500 mesh with two gigabit ports per node and Ethernet backhaul support.
products.description:
The Deco X15 is a dual-band AX1500 WiFi 6 mesh system. The listing claims coverage of up to 5,600 square feet for the pack, gives each unit two gigabit Ethernet ports and states that it supports Ethernet backhaul, which means the nodes can talk to each other over a cable instead of over the air.

It ranks last because it is the only pick here that the listing places in the $100 to $200 bucket, so it only fits this budget when discounted. If you can get it for less, the Ethernet backhaul is a real advantage. A wired link between nodes avoids the speed loss of wireless hops, which is the weakness of cheap mesh. The AX1500 class is also the slowest WiFi 6 tier in the guide.

Consider it if your house is already wired with Ethernet and you want the nodes linked by cable. Otherwise the X25 gives more for less.

whatMatters.detail: WiFi 6 is the newer standard and handles many simultaneous devices more efficiently, which matters in homes with phones, TVs, cameras and speakers all connected at once. WiFi 5, marked by the AC label, still works but ages faster. Look at the model name: AX means WiFi 6, AC means WiFi 5.

A node is one mesh unit. A single node suits a small apartment, two cover a medium home, and three handle larger or multi-story layouts. More nodes mean shorter hops between devices and the router. Count your floors and the far corners before you choose a pack.

Backhaul is the link between mesh nodes. Wireless backhaul shares airtime with your devices, so each hop reduces speed. Ethernet backhaul uses a cable, as the Deco X15 supports, and keeps full speed between nodes. Check the listing for the words Ethernet backhaul.

Labels like AX1800 and AX3000 add up the theoretical speed of both bands and are not what you will see on one device. They are useful only for comparing tiers. Match the tier to your internet plan, and do not pay for speed your plan cannot deliver.

A renewed unit is refurbished and resold, often with a shorter warranty and a return window set by the seller. It can be a bargain for networking gear that rarely wears out, but read the policy. If you want a full manufacturer warranty, look for a new listing.

faq.q: Can I mix different Deco models in one mesh?
faq.a: Often you can, but compatibility depends on the model families. Check the TP-Link compatibility list before mixing generations, since WiFi 5 and WiFi 6 nodes may not share every feature.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake with budget mesh systems?
faq.a: Placing nodes too far apart. Each node needs a decent signal from the one before it. Put them roughly halfway between the router and the dead zone, not in the dead zone itself.

faq.q: Is the X25 renewed pack worth it over a new S4?
faq.a: For most people, yes. You get WiFi 6 and three nodes for a similar budget. If you want a new unit with a full warranty, the S4 3-pack is the safer route, but it uses older WiFi 5 hardware.
It is straightforward. You connect the first unit to your modem, install the Deco app, and follow the prompts to add the other nodes. Most people finish in 15 to 20 minutes.

faq.q: Do I still need my old router?
faq.a: Usually not. A Deco unit replaces the router, though you may need to put your ISP's gateway in bridge mode so the two devices do not conflict. Your provider can explain how.

faq.q: Can a WiFi extender be a substitute for mesh?
faq.a: An extender repeats a signal and often halves the speed on the extended network. A mesh system manages one network across all nodes, which is smoother for roaming between rooms.

finalTake: For most budgets under $100, the renewed TP-Link Deco X25 3-pack is the best mesh WiFi system here, with WiFi 6 and three nodes. The Deco X55 is a better single node if your home is small and your internet is fast, and the Deco S4 3-pack is a sensible new-condition value option. The Deco X15 is worth a look only if it is on sale and your house has Ethernet. Node placement will matter more than the model you pick.
